questions.question_text:
Differentiating $F(x)=\dfrac{(9-4x)^{5}}{k}$ must give $f(x)=(9-4x)^{4}$.
What is the value of $k$?

options.why: Used $4$ as the coefficient and lost the negative sign of $a=-4$.
Used only the new power $5$ and ignored the coefficient $a=-4$ from the chain rule.
Used the original power $4$ instead of the new power $5$.

questions.solution_text:
$F(x)=\dfrac{(9-4x)^{5}}{k}$
Differentiate using the **chain rule**.
$F'(x)=\dfrac{5(9-4x)^{4}\times(-4)}{k}$
$=\dfrac{-20(9-4x)^{4}}{k}$
This equals $(9-4x)^{4}$ when $k=-20$.
